meta.title: Who really said "Eat a Live Frog Every Morning, and Nothing Worse Will Happen to You the Rest of the Day"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Mark Twain and not Émile Zola. Quote Investigator traces the maxim to Nicolas Chamfort in the 1790s; the modern English wording first appears unattributed in 1976.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Eat a Live Frog Every Morning, and Nothing Worse Will Happen to You the Rest of the Day'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Twain, not Zola — the maxim is Chamfort's, and today's English wording surfaces unattributed in 1976.

answer.label: Not Émile Zola — actually Nicolas Chamfort
answer.sourceLine: The saying is not Émile Zola’s, and it is not Mark Twain’s either. Quote Investigator traces it to the French aphorist Nicolas Chamfort, whose posthumous Oeuvres de Chamfort records M. de Lassay advising that one should swallow a toad every morning to fortify oneself against the disgust of the rest of the day. Zola’s 1896 essay “Le Crapaud” is where the toad becomes a live frog, and the exact English sentence people repeat today first turns up, with nobody’s name on it, on a sign quoted in 1976.

source.heading: Where the saying actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Tome IV, dated “L’an 3 de la République” (1794–95) · quote page 335
“Le Crapaud,” Le Figaro, 1896 — translated in The Speaker, 7 March 1896
An unattributed sign quoted in the Seattle Times, 17 December 1976 — and it says toad
Not Zola’s words — a modern English saying descended from Chamfort

source.excerpt: M. de Lassay, a very indulgent man, but with a great knowledge of society, said that we should swallow a toad every morning, in order to fortify ourselves against the disgust of the rest of the day, when we have to spend it in society.
trail: Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ concludes that the saying originated with Chamfort’s words, published around 1795, and cites Oeuvres de Chamfort, Tome IV, quote page 335, where the French reads “disait qu’il faudrait avaler un crapaud tous les matins.”

The same page records that Chamfort presents the advice as M. de Lassay’s rather than his own, and that Lassay “functioned as a mouthpiece for Chamfort.” QI credits Chamfort nonetheless, and we follow it.

On Zola: QI quotes an English rendering of his 1896 essay “Le Crapaud” from The Speaker of 7 March 1896 — “It is that you should learn to swallow a live frog every morning before sitting down to your daily task” — but offers no citation in which the saying is quoted as Zola’s own aphorism. QI gives no exact publication date for the Figaro essay, so neither do we.

On Twain: QI found no substantive evidence, and the earliest link it located is a Cleveland Plain Dealer column of 6 May 1988 — long after Twain’s death in 1910 — which hedged it as “I think it was Mark Twain who said, and if he didn’t he should have.” Note that Wikiquote’s Chamfort page ↗ does not carry the maxim either way, so QI’s citation is the whole of the attestation here.
source.excerptNote: That is the translation Quote Investigator quotes from Chamfort. The sentence in circulation today is a much shorter descendant of it, and the earliest instance QI found of that shorter English form — a sign quoted in the Seattle Times on 17 December 1976 — reads “Eat a live toad the first thing in the morning and nothing worse will happen to you the rest of the day.”

source.rightsNote: Chamfort’s French has long been in the public domain, but the English sentence on this page is not his: it is an anonymous twentieth-century rendering whose earliest known appearance is an unattributed 1976 newspaper item. With no identified author or first publication for that wording, no rights status can honestly be asserted for it.

author.name: Nicolas Chamfort
author.heading: About Nicolas Chamfort
author.bio: Sébastien-Roch Nicolas, known as Nicolas Chamfort, was a French writer remembered almost entirely for his epigrams and maxims, which John Stuart Mill ranked among the most brilliant of the modern era. He wrote plays and praise-pieces that nobody reads now, became secretary to Louis XVI’s sister Madame Élisabeth in 1784, and then secretary of the Jacobin club until August 1791. His maxims were gathered and published after his death in 1794, which is where this saying is found.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This one carries two false credits and one genuine ancestor, and the three are easy to run together.

items.why: Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence that Twain said or wrote it. The earliest link it located is a Cleveland Plain Dealer column of 6 May 1988 — long after Twain’s death in 1910 — and even that hedged: “I think it was Mark Twain who said, and if he didn’t he should have.”

items.scope: The other credit you will see
items.why: Zola genuinely wrote about swallowing a live frog each morning — his 1896 essay “Le Crapaud” is where the live frog enters the story, and an English rendering of it appeared in The Speaker on 7 March 1896. But Quote Investigator presents no citation quoting this saying as Zola’s own aphorism, and traces the maxim itself to Chamfort in the 1790s.
QI’s earliest citation is Oeuvres de Chamfort, Tome IV, quote page 335, dated “L’an 3 de la République” — 1794–95 — and its conclusion credits Chamfort. Read the chronology ↗.
Chamfort frames the advice as Lassay’s remark, not his own; QI notes that Lassay “functioned as a mouthpiece for Chamfort,” which is why the credit lands on Chamfort rather than on Lassay.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: a Chamfort maxim of the 1790s, re-pointed by Zola in 1896 and worn down into today’s English sentence by the 1970s — Quote Investigator’s full chronology ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The modern life of this saying is a productivity life. Quote Investigator’s chronology runs from Chamfort through Zola and a 1976 newspaper sign to Eat That Frog! in 2007, by which point the frog had become shorthand for doing your worst task first.

What got lost on the way is Chamfort’s actual point, which was social rather than managerial: swallow something disgusting early so that nothing you meet in company for the rest of the day can disgust you more.
detailsBody: QI’s dated citations run: Oeuvres de Chamfort (1794–95), Causeries du Lundi (1851), the Evening Post (1872), Hours with Men and Books (1877), Aphorisms (1877), The Speaker (1896), the Seattle Times (1976), the Cleveland Plain Dealer (1988), The Sunday Star (1989), 637 Best Things Anybody Ever Said (1990) and Eat That Frog! (2007).
context.pull: Chamfort’s toad was armour against company, not a to-do list.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI concludes the saying originated with Chamfort c.1795, cites Oeuvres de Chamfort Tome IV p.335, records M. de Lassay as the mouthpiece, quotes The Speaker 7 Mar 1896 for Zola’s live frog, gives the Seattle Times 17 Dec 1976 as earliest English wording, and finds no substantive Twain evidence (earliest link Cleveland Plain Dealer 6 May 1988).
Wikipedia gives Chamfort 1741-1794, French writer known for epigrams and aphorisms, secretary to Madame Elisabeth 1784 and secretary of the Jacobin club to Aug 1791.
Wikiquote's Chamfort page does NOT contain the toad/frog maxim (checked in raw wikitext).
Wikipedia page for Emile Zola exists and describes him (used as background only, not as support for the attribution).

presentation.pkitWarn: The slide-ready mistake: crediting this to Mark Twain, which is where most decks put it, or to Émile Zola, who only re-pointed it. Neither wrote the maxim; use the credit shown above.
